\chapter{Dijo --- The Stem That Breaks Its Own Rule}
\label{ch:dijo}
\hlchaptermodality{212}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can say what someone said, and say it in the plural without inventing a syllable.}

I can say what someone said, and say it in the plural without inventing a syllable.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[dijo]{dijo}

\label{lesson:ES-C57-dijo}



\begin{quote}
The strong pattern, once more: a stem that changed shape, and then endings that carry no stress. (\emph{Tuve}, \emph{tuvo}.)

One more stem is about to join them.
\end{quote}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: the stem is dij-}]
\emph{Decir} builds its past on \textbf{dij-}, and in the singular nothing is new at all:

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{} & \textbf{} \\
\midrule
\emph{tuve} · \emph{tuvo} & the stem you know \\
\emph{\textbf{dije}} · \emph{\textbf{dijo}} & the same endings, on a new stem \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

Unstressed at the end, exactly like the others. \emph{Dijo}, not \emph{dijó}.
\end{grammarlens}

\begin{cousinweb}
Latin said \emph{\textbf{dīxit}}. That \emph{x} stood for a {[}ks{]} — the sound at the end of English \emph{box}.

Old Spanish kept the letter and softened the sound: \emph{dixo}, with the \emph{x} said roughly like English \emph{sh}. Centuries later that sound hardened at the back of the mouth into the one \emph{j} spells today, and the spelling followed the sound. \textbf{dīxit $\to$ dixo $\to$ dijo.}

So the \emph{j} in \emph{dijo} is not a decoration. It is a Latin \emph{x}, wearing modern clothes.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: where it breaks the pattern}]
You learned the strong plural as stem plus \emph{-ieron}: \emph{tuvieron}, \emph{hicieron}, \emph{estuvieron}. Apply that here and you would get \emph{dijieron}.

\textbf{It is \emph{dijeron}.} The \emph{i} is gone.

The \emph{i} in \emph{-ieron} is not a full vowel — it is a glide, the \emph{y} sound of English \emph{yes}, leaning on the vowel after it. And Spanish does not keep a glide next to a sound already made in that part of the mouth. The \emph{j} was there first, so the glide goes.

This is not a fact about \emph{decir}. \textbf{Any strong stem ending in \emph{j} does it}, and you will meet more of them; when you do, the ending will already be familiar.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{dije}, \emph{dijo}, \emph{dijeron}
  \item \emph{tuvieron}, then \emph{dijeron}, and hear the difference
\end{itemize}

\emph{Twice through:}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
The stem? (\emph{\textbf{Dij-}}.) The \emph{they} form? (\emph{\textbf{Dijeron}} — no \emph{i}.)

And is that an exception you must memorise for this one verb, or a rule? (A \textbf{rule}, for every strong stem that ends in \emph{j}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
